feedback: When a child counts past 9 hundredths without naming 10 hundredths as 1 tenth, pause at the boundary and watch the ten small pieces reassemble into exactly one tenth; say '10 hundredths = 1 tenth' together.

If a child says the hundredth is bigger 'because 100 is bigger than 10', place the one hundredth against one tenth so the size difference is plain, and explain that splitting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller.
If a child denies the split pieces are hundredths, show that each of the ten tenths would hold ten such pieces, so 100 of them fill the whole, and name the repeatable 'divide by 10 again' action.
activities.intendedInsight: Hundredths come from dividing a tenth again by ten; ten hundredths rebuild one tenth and 100 hundredths make one whole. A hundredth is smaller than a tenth even though 100 is a bigger number than 10, because the same whole is split into more equal parts.
learnerActions: Start with a strip that is one whole, already partitioned into ten equal tenths.
Take a single tenth and cut (or subdivide) it into ten equal pieces; name one piece 'a hundredth' and write 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100.

Work out how many of these small pieces would fill the whole strip: each of the ten tenths holds ten hundredths, so 10 × 10 = 100. Connect this to 'a hundredth is one of a hundred equal parts of the whole'.
Count aloud in hundredths across the tenth boundary — 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 hundredths — and pause at 10 hundredths to say it is also 1 tenth.
Lay one hundredth directly beside one tenth and describe how much smaller the hundredth is.
activities.title: Split a tenth into ten hundredths

feedback: If a child places 7/100 by guessing, have them first mark the ten equal gaps between 0 and 1/10, then count to the seventh.
If the count continues '10 hundredths, 11 hundredths' without recognising 10 hundredths as 1 tenth, stop at the boundary and name both.
If a child treats 10 hundredths and 1 tenth as unrelated amounts, overlay them on the grid or line so they coincide.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting in hundredths and placing them between 0 and a tenth reinforces that each tenth holds exactly ten hundredths, so the count crosses cleanly into tenths.
learnerActions: Count up and down in hundredths from 3/100 to 12/100, saying each amount aloud.
When the count reaches 10 hundredths, name the equivalent in tenths (10 hundredths = 1 tenth), and note that the pattern continues (20 hundredths = 2 tenths).
On a number line running from 0 to 1/10, mark the equal gaps needed to show hundredths and place 7/100 in the correct spot.
Explain how many equal gaps lie between 0 and 1 tenth and why.
activities.title: Count in hundredths across the tenth boundary and place them on a line
